title: EUTxO-L2 interoperability: Connect Hydra and other L2s

ms.promise:
Objective: Create a prototype demonstrating the transfer of native Cardano assets between two isolated Hydra Heads using atomic payment transactions.
Details: Atomic transactions ensure that either all operations across the two Hydra Heads succeed or none do, preventing partial failures and avoiding liquidity traps. This milestone will validate whether native assets like USDM or ADA can move seamlessly across separate L2 instances. Using the classical approach of Hashed Timelock Contracts (HTLCs) a baseline payments scenario is established for next milestones. This milestone also includes a first design of the equivalent ad-hoc ledger approach (only for payments) outlined in the paper to get a first grasp on complexity of the approach.
Deliverables:
・Working code showcasing atomic asset + data transfers using HTLCs
・Draft of smart contracts for ad-hoc eUTxO ledger transactions (on-chain code)
・A technical report documenting the HTLC approach, how the ad-hoc ledger design works and any challenges encountered
ms.criteria:
・Demonstrated atomic payment transactions across two hydra heads with one intermediary using HTLCs
・Documented transaction design of above's scenario using an ad-hoc eUTxO ledger (nominal case, no dispute resolution)
ms.report:
We are pleased to announce the successful completion of Milestone #1 for the EUTxO-L2 interoperability: Connect Hydra and other L2s Catalyst project.
For this project we are working in the eutxo-l2-interop github repository. This repository holds all code related to the project, including documentation, infrastructure code to run the hydra heads, the onchain code for the HTLC validator and the offchain code to build and submit the transactions.
Milestone goals and proofs of completion
1. Develop an HTLC based solution for payments across Hydra Heads
The first task was to get a hydra head running with two nodes, we opted for offline mode to showcase the HTLC capabilities without having to deal with the constraints of a live testnet. We then updated the infrastructure to the desired two heads, each with a unique party (Alice in head A and Bob in head B) and a shared party (Ida is part of both heads).
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/1
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/5

We added the HTLC validator:
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/3

Then worked on the three main operations for the HTLC. Lock, allowing the user to specify the hash to use and the amount of lovelaces to deposit. Claim, allowing the receiver to provide the preimage and access the funds. And finally Refund, allowing the sender to retrieve the funds if the timeout has passed:
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/11
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/12
・https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/issues/13

2. Video showcasing the use
A video was recorded showing the flow of transferring funds from Alice in head A to Bob in head B, by using Ida as the intermediary. The video can be accessed here:
・https://www.loom.com/share/d483754d46a34786ab33879f08bfff3b?sid=8bf2436e-2cc7-4241-9402-4a8961e209ec

ms.promise:
Objective: Enable smart contract execution between distinct L2 ledgers, such as placing a bid on Midgard from a Hydra Head.
Details: This milestone explores cross-ledger calls where dApps on one L2 can interact with smart contracts on another. Example: a user on Hydra participates in an auction or lottery contract deployed on Midgard.
Deliverables:
・A demo of smart contract interactions across L2s using ad-hoc ledgers.
・A framework for structuring cross-ledger calls, including design patterns for request-response flows and transaction finality guarantees.
ms.criteria:
・Demonstrated a basic smart contract interaction (datum use) between two L2 ledgers.
・Documented how generic smart contract transactions map onto ad-hoc ledgers (nominal case, no dispute resolution)
ms.report:
RESUBMISSION: 
As one of the reviewers put it, we believe "the milestone has been completed successfully and in accordance with its exploratory objectives. The work establishes a solid foundation for maintaining momentum and advancing toward the next milestone.". We would like to address the feedback offered by other reviewers:
・No Midgard usage: At the time of implementing this project's Milestone 2, the Midgard project has not (yet) achieved an L2 node implementation (their MS5, scheduled end of March 2026 now). Feature-wise the Midgard ledger is expected to be on-par with Hydra ledgers and differ in the validator set, corresponding security guarantees and how funds are deposited/withdrawn. We will consider the existing specification when discussing the "non-happy" paths of enforcing L2 state onto L1 in our MS4. Should the Midgard testnet be available in time for our final milestone, we will demonstrate atomic transactions between Hydra and Migard (at least HTLC based, hopefully ad-hoc ledger based too).
・ Ad-hoc ledger design challenges: The nature of this proposal is very explorative and aims to verify feasibility of the ad-hoc ledger research paper. We underestimated the complexity of the published construction and have yet to find a concrete, implementable design (the paper was making quite some assumptions). We will continue exploration and hope to have a better answer in MS4 where not only the happy path, but also dispute resolution is to be considered. Evidence for the continued exploration of the concept can be seen in yesterday's Layer 2 working group recording: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1u2yLx-Qx--wNhDvElacF1f64Qw6sf-H1/view?t=710s. The interactions with other L2 protocol architects like George has been very rewarding and pointed us to potential ways forward (PTLCs or the signed redeemer idea discussed).

ms.promise:
Objective: Showcase payment transactions that flow through multiple L2 instances without breaking atomicity.
Details: Connected L2 ledgers can act as a payment aggregator where two or more L2s can settle transactions without requiring direct connections on dedicated state channels. This reduces the burden on users by minimizing the number of transfers they need to make between ledgers. This milestone is about single- and multi-step, atomic payments, ensuring that even if the payment involves several L2s, it either completes fully or reverts safely. Notably, this does not include any dynamic "routing" and purely static setups of Hydra heads and Midgard rollups, creating a blueprint for more complex multi-hop payment networks.
NOTE: This milestone deliberately combines the originally proposed milestones 4 and 5 from Ideascale, due to the great similarity between the central hub-and-spoke model (single-hop) and payments across multiple ledger (multi-hop) scenarios.
Deliverables:
・A working prototype demonstrating atomic transfers across three or more L2s.
・Documentation of various possible topologies and scenarios.
・Report comparing the efficiency of this model against point-to-point
ms.criteria:
・Payments can be executed across two two-party ledgers with a single inermediary using an ad-hoc multi-party ledger (single-hop).
・Payments can be executed across two multi-party ledgers with multiple intermediaries (single-hop).
・Payments can be executed across multiple L2 ledgers (multi-hop).
・Assuming nominal operation of L2 ledgers (no dispute resolution), transactions either succeed in all ledgers or none.
・Demonstrated scenarios on a public cardano testnet.

Milestone goals and proofs of completion
A. Output: A working prototype demonstrating atomic transfers across three or more L2s
Acceptance criteria:
・Payments can be executed across two multi-party ledgers with multiple intermediaries (single-hop)

Evidence:
As the first task, we defined which topologies we wanted to explore
・Two heads: already presented in milestone 2
・Single path: 3 heads connected in a chain. Allows multi-hop payments, multiple intermediaries.
・Hub and Spoke: one intermediary acting as hub, present in all heads. One-hop by “passing” from a spoke to any other spoke via the hub.

We implemented the infrastructure definition for running these two new topologies, along with the instructions for running them.
https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/pull/46
After that, we adapted and added new features to the UI demo presented in past milestone by
・Adding support for topology selection
・Automation of intermediaries: the HTLC form is now a Payment form, abstracting away the HTLC-across-L2s complexity

https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/pull/49
Finally, we recorded a demo showcasing the UI with these new features, showing the selection of different topologies and their payment paths, along with a demonstration of a two-hop payment flow in the single path topology.

Objective: Develop a mechanism for dispute resolution to ensure the integrity and liveness of cross-ledger operations, especially under adversarial conditions.
Details: Previous milestones have been relying on non-adversarial behavior (the happy path). The system will need to handle cases where one L2 attempts to withhold or delay part of a cross-ledger interaction. Midgard’s fraud proofs and Hydra’s state commitments provide the foundation for this milestone. This step ensures that transactions remain live and disputes can be resolved in favor of honest participants.
While for the hydra-only scenario, this research paper outlines a dispute mechanism, this milestone also aims to conduct some research & development of a similar, generalized mechanism that can be used in heterogenous setups between Hydra and Midgard. Due to the early development stage of Midgard, there is quite some uncertainty on this part and we can only commit to have this explored in a design document and (likely) not implemented.

We are pleased to announce the successful completion of Milestone #4 for the EUTxO-L2 interoperability: Connect Hydra and other L2s Catalyst project.
Milestone goals and proofs of completion
A. Output: Implementation of a dispute mechanism ensuring that cross-ledger operations cannot get stuck indefinitely.
Acceptance criteria:
・The dispute mechanism outlined in this paper is implemented for hydra-only setups.
・Explored a generalized dispute mechanism that also applies to heterogeneous use between Hydra and Midgard L2 (in writing, no implementation).
・Written documentation or recorded video explaining the dispute mechanism(s).

Evidence: 
The first task was to design and implement the onchain code for the dispute mechanism. For this, a new version of the verify/perform mechanism was idealized, and the validation corresponding to the dispute mechanism flow was implemented. Tests using the emulator were implemented as well.
https://github.com/cardano-scaling/eutxo-l2-interop/pull/54
Note that the emulator-based test suite, where plutus validation of L2 and L1 are emulated separately and a test driver maps UTxOs from the emulated L1 to L2 and back, underlines that the tested mechanism is indeed generalized. By abstracting the actual L2 implementation (like Hydra or Midgard), this test suite also proves that the system under test (the ad-hoc ledger design) would work for any eUTxO-based L2 ledger that provides the necessary interfaces: bridging

ms.promise:
Objective: Demonstrate a non-trivial example use case where smart contracts deployed across multiple L2s interact seamlessly.
Details: This milestone will feature a scenario where users on Hydra participate in a lottery contract running on Midgard. Participants will lock assets on Hydra, submit entries, and receive lottery results—all through cross-ledger interaction. This will prove the feasibility of building multi-L2 dApps. Also this final milestone includes wrapping up the technical report and the close-out video.
Deliverables:
・Full demonstration of a lottery contract with cross-ledger participation.
・Publicly released open-source code and a technical report outlining challenges, optimizations, and future improvements.
・Completed technical report, close-out report and close-out video
ms.criteria:
・Demonstrated interaction with a smart contract on Midgard from within a Hydra head.
・Example dApp is deployed to a public testnet and has a basic user interface.
・Example dApp is documented in the technical report.
・Technical report contains overall project status, encountered challenges and future work.
・Final close-out report is publicly available.
・Final close-out video is publicly available.
ms.report:
Re-submission: We have been reminded that there are special formatting guidelines required for the close-out report and close-out video. We hope that these two dedicated artifacts meet those requirements.
・Close-out Report: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1bpOHnNFx7GYQUG1ggmQXGORwy7VlJCF7/view
・Close-out Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p_Dd2e892wU

As for the closing of the lottery example dApp: we are still waiting for this upstream issue with Hydra to be resolved in the hydra-node version we have been using to open the Head on preprod (1.2.0). This problem only surfaces on preprod network (and not on local devnets) because it has a different slot length on Byron (while local devnets directly skip to the latest era). We are hoping to resolve and close it soon.
